subject: random effect of block in lavaan

messages.author: 03ebe38b8f11c7ec
messages.subject: random effect of block in lavaan
parts:
Dear lavaan users,
I have a model with entirely observed variables where all of them are measured in a complete block design. The variable "herb", an herbicide treatment, is applied in each block.. 
The model looks like this:
model <- '
  plantabun ~ herb
  plantrich ~ plantabun + herb
  mothabun ~ plantabun + herb
  mothrich ~ mothabun + plantabun + plantrich + herb
  '
fit <- sem(model, data = rich)
I would like to include the random effect of block in my model. Is there a straightforward way to do this?
Thanks,
Heather

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: random effect of block in lavaan
parts:
On 05/01/2015 04:27 PM, Heather Root wrote:
> I would like to include the random effect of block in my model. Is there
> a straightforward way to do this?

If you have the same number of observations in each block, yes, there is
a straightforward way.

You first need to reshape your data from 'long' to 'wide' format: all
the measurements within the same block should be on the same row in your
data.frame.

Then, you can allow for a 'random intercept' as in commonly done in
growth curve models

Yves.

messages.author: e5843eb415cfc782
messages.subject: Re: random effect of block in lavaan
parts:
Dear Heather, Yves, & lavaan users,

 

For my own analyses (I’m studying food web dynamics in California), I had a similar wish to include a random effect in my models.

My understanding is that it is possible to do so through the package lavaan.survey (Oberski D. 2014, see an introduction by the author to his package here: http://www.inside-r.org/packages/cran/lavaan.survey/docs/lavaan.survey). Yves advised so in 2012 in this discussion: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/lavaan/random$20effect/lavaan/3XhnM7CoaVU/JfqyOehlsyAJ. See also this more recent discussion: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/lavaan/random$20effect/lavaan/wjIKICrzHog/p6mLZCQ_M8YJ.

 

I won’t repeat here what is explained in the link provided above. However, to fully answer Heather original question, I’ll add a question regarding the exact use of lavaan.survey, in particular the step during which you describe your sampling design.

This involves the following code (as you can see following the above links):

       survey.design <- svydesign(ids=~your.block.column, prob=~1, data=your.dataset)

      #=> this would set Heather’s blocks as clusters.

However, the following is also feasible:

       survey.design <- svydesign(ids=~1, strata=~your.block.column, prob=~1, data=your.dataset)

      #=> this would set Heather’s blocks as stratum.

 

The issue is that, running my models with both options, the outcomes were very different. Using the “clusters” option increased a lot the fit between my model and my data. However, the fit between model and data slightly decreased when following the “stratum” option. This suggests that either option must be chosen in full understanding of its meaning and use in the model assessment.

 

Any help/clarification on how to choose between these options would be really helpful.

 

Cheers,

Nicolas

messages.author: 253141a6efac547e
messages.subject: Re: random effect of block in lavaan
parts:
My understanding is that lavaan.survey really follows a lot of the strictures of survey statistics, where there are far more knowns (e.g., total population size, probability of each sample being taken, etc.) rather than hierarchical linear models as we’re used to them, where these are not known. I could be wrong (feel free to correct me if so!)

Nicolas, you might also want to look into piecewiseSEM from Jon Lefcheck - https://github.com/jslefche/piecewiseSEM - which follows from both Bill Shipley and Jim Grace’s work.

-Jarrett
